summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency targets and throughput needs for Cascade Financial's in-app LLM features. Customer is weighing Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC) for compliance and latency guarantees. Key asks: p95 under 300ms for short chat flows, concurrency testing up to 200 concurrent users, streaming token/sec behavior, and token/sec cost estimates. Agreed to run benchmarks with three concurrency tiers and share security docs.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
questions: Can Redwood meet p95 <300ms for 128-token responses under 50 concurrency?
How does streaming latency compare to non-streaming at high concurrency?
What are typical tokens/sec and cost deltas for quantized models?
What telemetry and audit logs are available for Private deployments?
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros?
[00:07] Hannah Lee: Hannah here, Head of ML at Cascade, we own the recommendation and chat surfaces. Jon and Priya are on for infra and security.
[00:15] Jon Ortiz: morning, jon, platform eng.
[00:18] Maya Patel: Great, Lucas, quick pitch?
[00:21] Lucas Chen: Yeah hi, I'm Lucas, SE at Redwood. We'll focus today on latency and throughput for your use case — p95 targets, concurrency, streaming behavior, token/sec benchmarks. Apologies if auto transcript messes names.
[00:35] Hannah Lee: No worries. Context — we have an in-app chat assistant used for transactional workflows, usually short responses ~50-150 tokens, and a reranking job for search. Our internal goal is p95 below 300ms for short flows; for longer summarizations 800-1000ms is OK. We're evaluating Hosted for speed to market, Dedicated for predictable latency, and Private for compliance.
[01:00] Priya Nair: Also we need audit logs and KMS integration, and VPC peering for Private. SOC 2 is required.
[01:10] Lucas Chen: Totally — Redwood has Hosted with low-latency profiles, Dedicated reserved GPU pools, and Private (VPC) with customer-managed networking and KMS/HSM integrations. For the numbers: what concurrency are you planning?
[01:20] Hannah Lee: Peak concurrency is around 200 simultaneous chat sessions during spikes. Average is more like 30-40. We also do some bulk embedding and reranking off-hours.
[01:30] Maya Patel: Great, so p95 <300ms at 200 concurrency for 50-150 token outputs is the ask, plus streaming behavior. That's challenging on Hosted unless we tune batching and caching. Lucas can you walk through tradeoffs?
[01:44] Lucas Chen: Sure. First, streaming adds an initial token latency advantage because partial tokens are sent as generated; but end-to-end p95 can still be dominated by model setup and KV cache warmups. On dedicated hardware we can reserve continuous batching parameters to keep latency predictable. On Hosted we use smart routing and fallback to cheaper variants when capacity is constrained which can introduce variability.
[02:10] Jon Ortiz: Any ballpark tokens/sec or tokens-per-second numbers we should expect? We run LLMs for chat and rerank, want to compare cost.
[02:18] Lucas Chen: Tokens/sec is model and hardware-dependent — for a 7B quantized model on A100-ish equivalent we see ~400-800 tokens/sec single-stream on optimized runtime, multi-stream concurrency reduces per-stream tokens/sec but increases aggregate throughput. For 70B on GPU it's lower per-stream. For p95 targets the critical bits are sequence length and KV cache reuse. If your average is short 100 tokens, it's easier.
[02:45] Hannah Lee: Are there published perf profiles? We want a sense of cost per 1M tokens at our expected latency envelope.
[02:52] Lucas Chen: We have a model catalog with verified perf profiles; I'll link it. Cost modeling depends on batching windows and caching — Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization and batch configs.
[03:05] Priya Nair: On Private, latency with VPC peering — do you have network diagrams? TLS, mutual TLS? We need to show audit logs to compliance.
[03:15] Ravi Kumar: For Private we provide a customer control plane with VPC connectors; KMS integration for keys, audit logs shipped to your SIEM. There is some additional network hop but you control the topology — latency can be similar to Dedicated depending on colo layout.
[03:30] Hannah Lee: Ok. Real question: will Hosted hit p95 <300ms at 200 conc for 100-token responses?
[03:38] Lucas Chen: Short answer: unlikely consistently without Dedicated. Hosted can often meet <300ms at lower conc (20-50), but at 200 concurrency we usually recommend Dedicated reserved pools unless your traffic is highly spiky and you can tolerate occasional p95 regressions. We can do a pilot to measure.
[03:55] Maya Patel: Let's talk bench plan — Hannah, can you provide prompt sets and success criteria (p95 numbers)?
[04:02] Hannah Lee: Yes, we'll provide three tiers: 1) low conc 20-50, 2) medium 100-120, 3) high 180-220. For each tier we want p50/p95/p99 and streaming behavior — e.g., first byte time and time to last token.
[04:18] Lucas Chen: For the benchmark we'll run models in the catalog: a quantized 7B, a 13B and a 34/70 hybrid if you want to test quality vs latency. We'll measure tokens/sec, end-to-end tail latencies, and cost per 1M tokens.
[04:33] Jon Ortiz: We'll want test harness to run from our VPC (for Private/Dedicated) and from public net (for Hosted). Can you provide an agent or runner?
[04:42] Lucas Chen: Yes, we'll share a lightweight harness and a beats-style load generator repo. I'll attach the repo link in follow up.
[04:50] Hannah Lee: A few clarifying Qs — how does streaming scale when you have many open streams? Does it maintain first-byte latency or degrade?
[04:59] Lucas Chen: Great question. Streaming maintains first-byte latency better at lower conc, but when you have many concurrent open long-lived streams you hit scheduling and GPU SM saturation; that increases per-stream jitter. Continuous batching tries to group tokens across streams to maintain throughput but it can increase first-byte if batch windows are too long. We can tune batch windows and target latency SLOs.
[05:20] Priya Nair: On security: what's in the audit logs? Can logs be forwarded to Splunk? And encryption at rest with customer KMS?
[05:28] Ravi Kumar: Logs include request/response metadata (no raw user content unless configured), model version, route, timestamp, and operator actions. Logs can be forwarded to Splunk or S3; Private can be set to use your KMS keys for model artifacts and any persisted cache. We'll share SOC2 and architecture docs.
[05:45] Maya Patel: Any competitor risk?
[05:47] Hannah Lee: We're looking at Anthropic for chat quality and OpenAI for speed; Bedrock for enterprise integrations. Replicate for lower-cost hosting.
[05:55] Lucas Chen: Noted. We focus on predictable inference economics and tooling for rollouts — can do canary and automatic fallbacks to cheaper variants if you want to prioritize availability during spikes.
[06:06] Jon Ortiz: For Dedicated what does provisioning look like and lead times?
[06:10] Maya Patel: Lucas?
[06:12] Lucas Chen: Dedicated has a reserved pool model; we size based on your desired concurrency and throughput. Typical lead time for capacity allocation is 2-6 weeks depending on region and capacity. For Private on-prem it's longer. For initial pilot we can provision smaller Dedicated or use Hosted for quick testing.
[06:28] Hannah Lee: Let's record the success criteria again: p95 <300ms for 100-token average at 200 conc, first byte <120ms for streaming ideally, and cost under a specified per-token threshold — we'll provide exact number.
[06:42] Ravi Kumar: We'll also need SAML SSO and RBAC for admin controls.
[06:46] Lucas Chen: We support SAML, SCIM, and granular RBAC in Console.
[06:51] Hannah Lee: Good. Questions from our side: do you do local KV cache warmup strategies and prefix caching for sessions?
[06:58] Lucas Chen: Yes, Redwood supports prefix caching and KV caching that persists across sessions depending on routing. That helps p95 for repeated user prompts.
[07:08] Maya Patel: Ok, recap and next steps — Maya to send pricing and Dedicated sizing, Lucas to send bench plan and repo, Cascade to send prompts and SLOs, and we'll schedule benchmark week. Any final notes?
[07:22] Jon Ortiz: Please include expected tokens/sec numbers for each model in the doc.
[07:27] Lucas Chen: Will do.
[07:30] Priya Nair: Look forward to SOC2 docs.
[07:32] Maya Patel: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email.
[07:35] (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: occasional mis-attribution and minor word errors from auto transcription, e.g., "KV cache" occasionally transcribed as "K V cache" and product names slightly off.
